'''Nick Holonyak Jr.''' (November 3, 1928 – September 18, 2022) was an American [[electrical engineer]]. He is noted particularly for his 1962 invention and first demonstration of a semiconductor [[laser diode]] that emitted visible light. This device was the forerunner of the first generation of commercial [[light-emitting diode]]s (LEDs). He was then working at a [[General Electric]] research laboratory near [[Syracuse, New York]]. He left General Electric in 1963 and returned to his alma mater, the [[University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign]], where he later became John Bardeen Endowed Chair in Electrical and Computer Engineering and Physics.<ref name=Schubert>{{cite book |title=Light-Emitting Diodes |last=Schubert |first=E. Fred |date=2018 |edition=3 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |pages=2–6 |quote=Another important step in the development of GaAs<sub>y</sub>P<sub>1–y</sub> (or simply GaAsP) LEDs occurred in 1962 when Holonyak and Bevacqua (1962) reported on the emission of coherent visible light from GaAsP p-n junctions at low temperatures (77 K) under pulsed current injection. The emission of coherent light was limited to low temperatures. At room temperature, the devices worked as LEDs and emitted incoherent visible red light. The 1962 publication is considered a milestone in the development of pn-junction LEDs made from III–V semiconductors emitting in the visible wavelength range (Holonyak, 1987).|isbn=9780986382666 |oclc= |url=https://sites.google.com/semiconductor-consulting.com/led-book-3rd-edition}}</ref><ref name="aip.org">{{cite web|url=https://www.aip.org/history-programs/niels-bohr-library/oral-histories/30533|title=Nick Holonyak|date=February 19, 2015|website=www.aip.org|language=en|access-date=April 6, 2019|archive-date=September 12, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180912022216/https://www.aip.org/history-programs/niels-bohr-library/oral-histories/30533|url-status=live}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
Nick Holonyak Jr. was born on November 3, 1928, in [[Zeigler, Illinois]],<ref>{{cite web |title=Nick Holonyak |url=https://www.pbs.org/transistor/album1/addlbios/holonyak.html |website=www.pbs.org |access-date=September 19, 2022 |archive-date=May 27, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220527135743/http://www.pbs.org/transistor/album1/addlbios/holonyak.html |url-status=live}}</ref> to [[Rusyns|Rusyn]] immigrants.<ref name="aip.org"/><ref>{{cite web |url=http://distributedmuseum.blogspot.com/2013/10/nick-holonyak-jr.html |title=Illinois Distributed Museum – Nick Holonyak, Jr. |publisher=IDM |website=IDM Illinois Distributed Museum |access-date=January 17, 2015 |archive-date=March 17, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150317011452/http://distributedmuseum.blogspot.com/2013/10/nick-holonyak-jr.html |url-status=live}}</ref> The family moved to [[Glen Carbon, Illinois]] where his father worked in a [[coal mine]]. Holonyak was the first member of his family to receive any type of formal schooling.<ref name="afterglow"/>  He once worked 30 straight hours on the [[Illinois Central Railroad]] before realizing that a life of hard labor was not what he wanted and he would prefer to go to school instead. According to a ''[[Chicago Tribune]]'' article in 2003, "The cheap and reliable semiconductor lasers critical to DVD players, bar code readers and scores of other devices owe their existence in some small way to the demanding workload thrust upon Downstate railroad crews decades ago."<ref name="knightridder">{{cite news |title=Nice Guys Can Finish As Geniuses at University of Illinois in Urbana-Champaign |last=Von |first=Jon |url= http://www.highbeam.com/doc/1G1-96919218.html |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20110516180527/http://www.highbeam.com/doc/1G1-96919218.html |url-status= usurped |archive-date= May 16, 2011 |work=Chicago Tribune |date=January 25, 2003 |via=[[HighBeam Research]] |url-access=subscription |access-date=January 17, 2015}}</ref>

Holonyak earned his [[Bachelor of Science]] (1950), [[Master of Science]] (1951), and [[Doctor of Philosophy]] (1954) degrees in Electrical Engineering from the [[University of Illinois]], where he was the first graduate student of [[John Bardeen]]. In 1954, Holonyak went to [[Bell Telephone Laboratories]], where he worked on silicon-based electronic devices. From 1955 to 1957, he served with the [[U.S. Army Signal Corps]].<ref>{{Cite web|title= Nick Holonyak Jr. |url=https://grainger.illinois.edu/alumni/hall-of-fame/nick-holonyak|url-status=live|publisher=University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260929164857/https://grainger.illinois.edu/alumni/hall-of-fame/nick-holonyak|archive-date=September 29, 2026|access-date=October 16, 2026}}</ref><ref name=obit/>

== Career and research ==
From 1957 to 1963, Holonyak was a scientist at [[General Electric]]'s Advanced Semiconductor Laboratory near [[Syracuse, New York]]. Here he invented, fabricated, and demonstrated the first visible light [[laser diode]] on October 9, 1962. He grew crystals of the alloy GaAs<sub>0.60</sub>P<sub>0.40</sub>; a GaAs laser diode that worked in the infrared had recently been demonstrated by his General Electric colleague [[Robert N. Hall]]. The GaAs<sub>0.60</sub>P<sub>0.40</sub> laser diode worked at low temperatures, but the device still functioned as a light-emitting diode at room temperature.<ref name=APL62>{{cite journal |first1=Nick |last1=Holonyak Jr. |first2=S. F. |last2=Bevacqua |journal=Applied Physics Letters |title=Coherent (visible) Light Emission from Ga(As<sub>1−x</sub>P<sub>x</sub>) Junctions |date=December 1, 1962 |volume=1 |issue=4 |page=82 |doi=10.1063/1.1753706|bibcode=1962ApPhL...1...82H }}</ref> The demonstration of red light emission from the diode inspired the article "Light of Hope – or Terror" in ''[[Reader's Digest]]''. GaAsP was the material used for the first generation of commercial LEDs that came to market a few years later.<ref>{{cite news |first=Harland |last=Manchester |work=Reader's Digest |title=Light of Hope – or Terror |date=February 1963 |page=97 |quote=The latest dramatic laser discoveries, made by General Electric, may someday make the electric light obsolete. If these plans work out, the lamp of the future may be a speck of metal the size of a pencil-point which will be practically indestructible, will never burn out, and will convert at least ten times as much current into light as does today's bulb.}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.ieeeghn.org/wiki/index.php/Nicholas_Holonyak,_Jr. |title=Nick Holonyak, Jr. – Biography |publisher=IEEE |website=IEEE Global History Network |access-date=January 17, 2015 |archive-date=February 19, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140219033714/http://www.ieeeghn.org/wiki/index.php/Nicholas_Holonyak,_Jr. |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Nick Holonyak, Jr., six decades in pursuit of light |date=May 4, 2012 |last1=Kubetz |first1=Rick |publisher=University of Illinois |url=https://grainger.illinois.edu/news/stories/2012-05-04-nick-holonyak-jr-six-decades-pursuit-light |access-date=September 17, 2022 |archive-date=October 21, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211021084746/https://grainger.illinois.edu/news/stories/2012-05-04-nick-holonyak-jr-six-decades-pursuit-light}}</ref><ref name="chisuntimes">{{cite news | title=U. of I.'s Holonyak out to take some of Edison's luster |last= Wolinsky |first=Howard | date =February 5, 2005 | url =http://www.highbeam.com/doc/1P2-1562141.html | archive-url =https://web.archive.org/web/20160225081413/https://www.highbeam.com/doc/1P2-1562141.html | url-status =usurped | archive-date =February 25, 2016 | work=Chicago Sun-Times | via=HighBeam Research | url-access=subscription | access-date = January 17, 2015}}</ref>

In 1963, Holonyak became a professor at the University of Illinois.<ref name=Damery>{{cite web |url=http://www.ece.illinois.edu/newsroom/article/2575 |first=Jonathan |last=Damery |date=August 5, 2013 |title=Holonyak retires after 50 years in ECE |publisher=University of Illinois |access-date=January 17, 2015 |archive-date=February 8, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150208225650/http://www.ece.illinois.edu/newsroom/article/2575 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |author=Grainger Engineering Office of Marketing and Communications |url=https://mntl.illinois.edu/news/10981 |title=Illinois faculty, former students honor Nick Holonyak legacy in celebration of his birthday &#124; Holonyak Micro & Nanotechnology Lab &#124; UIUC |publisher=Mntl.illinois.edu |date=December 22, 2018 |accessdate=September 18, 2022 |archive-date=April 22, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220422224323/https://mntl.illinois.edu/news/10981 |url-status=live}}</ref> In 1993, he was named the John Bardeen Endowed Chair Professor of Electrical and Computer Engineering and Physics.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://lemelson.mit.edu/resources/nick-holonyak |title=Nick Holonyak &#124; Lemelson |publisher=Lemelson.mit.edu |date=November 3, 1928 |accessdate=September 18, 2022 |archive-date=January 26, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210126172123/https://lemelson.mit.edu/resources/nick-holonyak |url-status=live}}</ref> He investigated methods for manufacturing [[quantum dot laser]]s. He and Dr. [[Milton Feng]] ran a transistor laser research center at the university funded by $6.5&nbsp;million from the [[United States Department of Defense]] through [[DARPA]].<ref name="businessweek"/> Holonyak retired from Illinois in 2013.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.pjstar.com/story/news/2013/08/07/led-inventor-retires-from-u/42432906007/ |title=LED inventor retires from U. of Illinois |publisher=Pjstar.com |date=August 7, 2013 |archive-date=September 19, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220919131040/https://www.pjstar.com/story/news/2013/08/07/led-inventor-retires-from-u/42432906007/ |url-status=live}}</ref>

Ten of his 60 former doctoral students have developed new uses for LED technology at [[Philips Lumileds Lighting Company]] in [[Silicon Valley]].<ref name="chisuntimes"/>

== Inventions ==
[[File:GE Electronics Laboratory.jpg|thumb|right |alt=Photograph of a two-story building with a tan brick facade and green copper roofing. A few steps lead up to wide glass doors. Signage above the doors reads "ELECTRONICS LABORATORY" |The former General Electric laboratory near Syracuse, New York, where Holonyak demonstrated red light from a diode laser and light-emitting diode in 1962.]]

In addition to introducing the III-V alloy LED, Holonyak held 41 [[patent]]s.  His other inventions include the red-light [[semiconductor]] laser, usually called the [[laser diode]] (used in [[CD player|CD]] and [[DVD player]]s and [[cell phone]]s) and the [[silicon controlled rectifier|shorted emitter p-n-p-n switch]] (used in light dimmers and power tools).<ref name="afterglow">{{cite news |title= After Glow |publisher=Illinois Alumni Magazine |date=May–June 2007}}</ref>

In 2006, the [[American Institute of Physics]] decided on the five most important papers in each of its journals since it was founded 75 years ago. Two of these five papers, in the journal ''[[Applied Physics Letters]]'', were co-authored by Holonyak. The first one, co-authored with S. F. Bevacqua in 1962, announced the creation of the first visible-light laser diode.<ref name=APL62 /> The second, co-authored primarily with [[Milton Feng]] in 2005, announced the creation of a [[transistor laser]] that can operate at [[room temperature]]s.  Holonyak predicted that his LEDs would replace the [[incandescent light bulb]] of [[Thomas Edison]] in the February 1963 issue of ''[[Reader's Digest]]'', and as LEDs improve in quality and efficiency they are [[Phase-out of incandescent light bulbs|gradually replacing incandescents]] as the bulb of choice.<ref name="businessweek">{{cite news |title=Nick Holonyak: He Saw The Lights |last=Port |first=Otis |url=http://www.businessweek.com/magazine/content/05_21/b3934030.htm |work=Business Week |date=May 23, 2005 |access-date=January 17, 2015 |archive-date=June 27, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120627002816/http://www.businessweek.com/magazine/content/05_21/b3934030.htm |url-status=dead}}</ref>

== Personal life ==
Holonyak and his wife, Katherine, were married for over 60 years. He died on September 18, 2022, in [[Urbana, Illinois]], at the age of 93.<ref name=obit>{{cite web|title=Nick Holonyak Jr., pioneer of LED lighting, dies|last=Ahlberg Touchstone|first=Liz|url=https://news.illinois.edu/view/6367/1920044460 |date=September 18, 2022|publisher=University of Illinois News Bureau|access-date=September 18, 2022|archive-date=September 19, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220919031625/https://news.illinois.edu/view/6367/1920044460|url-status=live}}</ref>

Many colleagues expressed their belief that Holonyak deserved the Nobel Prize for his invention of the GaAsP laser and LED.  On this subject, he said: "It's ridiculous to think that somebody owes you something. We're lucky to be alive, when it comes down to it."<ref name="afterglow"/> In October 2014, Holonyak reversed his stance by stating "I find this one insulting" in reaction to news that the inventors of the blue LED were awarded the 2014 [[Nobel Prize in Physics]], instead of his fellow LED researchers.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.eeworldonline.com/led-inventor-insulted-feels-work-bypassed-by-nobel/ |title=LED Inventor Insulted, Feels Work Bypassed By Nobel |first1=David |last1=Mercer |agency=Associated Press |date=October 8, 2014 |website=Electrical Engineering News and Products |access-date=September 18, 2022 |archive-date=September 19, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220919131044/https://www.eeworldonline.com/led-inventor-insulted-feels-work-bypassed-by-nobel/ |url-status=live}}</ref>

== Commemoration ==
* 1997: The Optical Society of America (now [[Optica (society)|Optica]]) created the [[Nick Holonyak, Jr. Award]] in his honor.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Nick Holonyak, Jr. Award|url=https://www.optica.org/get_involved/awards_and_honors/awards/award_descriptions/nickholonyak/|url-status=live|website=www.optica.org|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250627054155/https://www.optica.org/get_involved/awards_and_honors/awards/award_descriptions/nickholonyak/|archive-date=2025-06-27|access-date=2025-12-27}}</ref>
* 2005: Inducted as a Laureate of [[The Lincoln Academy of Illinois]] and awarded the Order of Lincoln (the State's highest honor) by the [[Governor of Illinois]] in the area of Science.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://thelincolnacademyofillinois.org/4632-2/#toggle-id-11|title=Laureates by Year |work=The Lincoln Academy of Illinois |language=en-US|access-date=March 7, 2016|archive-date=September 23, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150923204516/http://thelincolnacademyofillinois.org/4632-2/#toggle-id-11|url-status=live}}</ref>
* June 2006: Two of Holonyak's papers were chosen by the editors of ''Applied Physics Letters'' as among the five most important published since the journal's founding in 1962.<ref>{{cite news |title=Illinois physicists produce two most important scientific papers |date=June 5, 2006 |work=phys.org |url=https://phys.org/news/2006-06-illinois-physicists-important-scientific-papers.html}}</ref>
* November 9, 2007: [[Historical marker]] installed on the University of Illinois campus recognizing his development of the quantum-well laser. It is located on the Bardeen Engineering Quadrangle near where the old Electrical Engineering Research Laboratory used to stand.<ref name="UIEngineeringNews200711">{{Cite web|url=https://ece.illinois.edu/newsroom/news/2574|title=Holonyak historical marker unveiled|first=Grainger Engineering Office of Marketing and|last=Communications|website=ece.illinois.edu|access-date=September 18, 2022|archive-date=April 12, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210412123317/https://ece.illinois.edu/newsroom/news/2574|url-status=live}}</ref>
* 2008: Inducted into the [[National Inventors Hall of Fame]] (Announced February 14, 2008) (May 2–3, 2008 at Akron, Ohio).<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.engr.uiuc.edu/news/?xId=072808800672 |title=News {{!}} Engineering at Illinois {{!}} University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign<!-- Bot generated title --> |access-date=June 10, 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200314195955/https://grainger.illinois.edu/news |archive-date=March 14, 2020 |url-status=dead}}</ref>
* September 2018: Village of [[Glen Carbon, Illinois]], placed an honorary street sign on behalf of Holonyak, a former resident.<ref>{{cite web |last=Sommerhof |first=John |url=https://www.thetelegraph.com/news/article/Glen-Carbon-names-first-honorary-street-13058860.php |title=Glen Carbon names first honorary street designation |publisher=Thetelegraph.com |date=July 9, 2018 |accessdate=September 18, 2022 |archive-date=July 9, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180709083726/https://www.thetelegraph.com/news/article/Glen-Carbon-names-first-honorary-street-13058860.php |url-status=live}}</ref>
